content: The study by van de Berg et al. (2021), based on the 2019 KNCV report funded by the TB Alliance, evaluated the feasibility of using the BPaL regimen for pre-XDR tuberculosis patients compared to the longer WHO-recommended regimen. However, the findings from this study are only partially applicable to the current context. The study highlighted potential barriers to implementation, including the need for drug safety monitoring and drug susceptibility testing (DST). The limited availability of drugs in the BPaLC regimen for DST and the lack of data on the critical concentration of pretomanid for DST were also noted as challenges. Despite these barriers, the panel concluded that the reduced duration, complexity, and associated workload of the BPaL regimen make its implementation probably feasible. The WHO 2022 guidelines recommend a 6-month treatment regimen consisting of bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, and moxifloxacin (BPaLM) for MDR/RR-TB patients, with or without fluoroquinolone resistance, provided they have not been previously exposed to bedaquiline and linezolid or have been exposed for less than one month. This recommendation is based on evidence from the TB-PRACTECAL and ZeNix trials, which provided new data on the efficacy and safety of shorter, all-oral regimens. MDR/RR-TB remains a significant global health challenge due to poor management of drug-susceptible TB and the transmission of drug-resistant strains. While MDR/RR-TB is treatable, the regimens are often long, toxic, and expensive. The interest in shorter, safer, and more effective regimens has driven research into novel treatment options. In 2016, WHO recommended a standardized 9-month regimen containing an injectable agent, which was shorter than the previous 18–20-month standard of care. However, evidence of permanent toxic effects from injectable agents has led to the development of injectable-sparing regimens. In 2019, WHO reviewed and recommended an all-oral 9-month bedaquiline-containing regimen based on observational data from South Africa. This regimen was further modified in 2022 to include 2 months of linezolid (600 mg) instead of 4 months of ethionamide. The Nix-TB study, conducted by the Global TB Alliance, evaluated a 6-month regimen of bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid (BPaL) for MDR/RR-TB patients with additional fluoroquinolone resistance. While the study showed promising results, limitations in study design, small sample size, and observed adverse events prevented the panel from recommending global programmatic implementation until further evidence is generated. In the 2020 WHO guidelines, the BPaL regimen was recommended for use under operational research conditions. The COVID-19 pandemic has significantly impacted TB services, reversing years of progress. There was an 18% global decline in the number of newly diagnosed TB cases in 2020, returning to 2012 levels. Reduced access to TB diagnosis and treatment has led to an increase in TB-related deaths. The number of people receiving treatment for drug-resistant TB also declined by 15% between 2019 and 2020. Despite these challenges, treatment success rates for MDR/RR-TB have steadily improved, reaching 59% globally in 2018. The TB-PRACTECAL trial compared the BPaLC regimen to the BPaL 600–300 regimen. The evidence regarding the effects of BPaLC on all outcomes remains highly uncertain. The panel judged that BPaLC may have small desirable effects but noted the very low certainty of the evidence. Similarly, the undesirable effects of BPaLC were judged to be small, with very low certainty of evidence. Several limitations were identified in the TB-PRACTECAL trial. These include imbalances in measured covariates (e.g., gender, past TB treatment, smear status, fluoroquinolone resistance) due to the small number of participants in each group, potential unmeasured confounding, and the lack of blinding of patients, caregivers, and outcome adjudicators, which may introduce bias. The trial was stopped early for benefit, with fewer than 200 events, which can also introduce bias. Additionally, multiple comparator regimens were used across sites, contributing to inconsistencies in treatment outcomes between countries (e.g., Belarus, South Africa, Uzbekistan). The small sample size (n=64 and n=60 in intervention and comparator groups, respectively) and very few events in outcomes of interest caused serious imprecision, leading to downgrading of evidence certainty. The panel emphasized the need for further research to address these limitations and generate robust evidence to inform future recommendations.
